info.title: Pidgeon API
info.description:
An email inbox API for AI agents. Inboxes your code creates in one call, threads that carry state, and sending from a domain you own.

Every response is `{ data }`, a page is `{ data, has_more, next_cursor }`, and a failure is `{ error: { code, message } }`. There is no third envelope.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Any string unique to this attempt, reused on its retries. A repeat with the same key and the same request returns the first answer with `Idempotent-Replay: true` and does nothing — no second email. The same key with a different request is a `409`. Kept for 24 hours; a failure is not kept, so a retry after one runs.

post.summary: Decide what happens to a sender
post.description:
`value` is an address or a domain and the string says which: `billing@acme.com` matches one person, `acme.com` matches everybody there. **The more specific rule wins**, and an address’s own rule wins over a workspace-wide one. Adding **replaces** any rule already there for that value.

`action` is `reject`, `spam`, `trash`, `archive` or `inbox`. **`reject` refuses before the message is stored** — no row, no thread, no storage charged and no webhook — which is what an address nobody will ever open wants. The other four file it, and `inbox` means *never classify this sender as spam*.

**It is not a security control.** The `From:` header is written by the sender, and anybody blocked can change it for the price of a new address. What this buys is not paying for mail from senders who have not bothered.

Without `after`, it first looks back 2 minutes and returns the newest matching message from then, because a code often lands before the call is made; narrow it with `from`, `subject_contains` or `has_code` so an earlier email is not taken for the one you want, or pass `after=now` to wait only for new mail. get.description:
The same events a webhook delivers, readable after the fact — so a missed delivery is recoverable without replaying anything.

**Two directions.** `cursor` pages backwards through history, newest first, which is what a dashboard shows. `after` tails the log forwards, oldest first, which is what a caller that cannot receive a webhook does: ask for everything since the last event you saw, act on it, and keep the last `created_at` as the next cursor. Naming both is refused — they are different reads.

**Starting from nothing: pass `after=1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`.** With neither parameter this answers newest first, so a first-time consumer that takes the last row as its high-water mark stores the *oldest* event in the log and never advances. Any timestamp at or before the oldest event you hold will do; the epoch is the one nobody has to think about.

A forward page is ordered oldest first precisely so its **last** row is the high-water mark to resume from; `next_cursor` is that row either way.

get.description:
The event log over a WebSocket — `wss://pidgeon.ai/api/v1/events/socket` — with the same `type`, `identity_id` and `after` as `GET /events/stream`. All frames are JSON text.

**Authenticate** with the `Authorization` header on the upgrade, or — from a browser, which cannot set one — send `{"type":"auth","api_key":"pgn_live_…"}` as the first message within ten seconds. Never put the key in the URL.

**The server sends** `{"type":"ready","cursor"}`, then `{"type":"event","event":Event}` per event, oldest first. Before about 280 seconds it sends `{"type":"reconnect","cursor"}` and closes with 4000: reconnect with `after` set to that cursor and nothing is missed. 4401 means no key or a bad one; 4500 means the read failed — reconnect with the last cursor you saw.

Like the stream, it polls the log on our side of the wire every two seconds.

get.description:
The event log held open, for a caller that cannot host a webhook endpoint — a script on a laptop, a notebook, an agent runtime with no public address.

**Server-sent events.** Each message carries the event as `data`, the event type as `event:`, and the cursor to resume from as `id:`. Authentication, filtering by `type` and `identity_id`, and the `after` cursor are all exactly as on `GET /events` — this is that read, held open.

**Reconnection is automatic and lossless.** A compliant client resends the last `id:` it saw as `Last-Event-ID`, which is preferred over `after`, so a dropped connection resumes with no gap and no repeat. The connection closes itself after about 280 seconds so that the last thing you receive is a cursor rather than a socket error; reconnect and carry on.

**It polls, every two seconds, on our side of the wire.** No push exists in the database. What this buys is one held connection instead of a request from your network on a timer, and being woken only when something happened.

patch.summary: Change some of it, and leave the rest
patch.description: An omitted field survives; `null` clears it. Both are needed, because "I am not touching the subject" and "there is no subject" are different instructions.

from.description: An address on a domain you own, and one this key may send from.

to.description: One address or several. A string is accepted for the single case.

cc.description: Copied, and visible to everybody who receives the message.

bcc.description: Copied, and visible to nobody else.

subject.description: Left off a reply, where the thread already has one.

text.description: The plain-text body. Send this even when you send `html` — some clients only read it.

schema.description: A URL naming what `body` is, such as `https://schema.org/Invoice`.

body.description: The JSON itself. Up to 64 KB once serialised.

anyOf.description: Typed data: structured JSON sent beside the text, for software at the other end to read as fields. Travels as its own part; it is never mixed into the text.

data.description: Typed data: `{ schema, body }`, where `schema` is a URL naming what `body` is and `body` is up to 64 KB of JSON. Sent as its own part beside the text, never mixed into it.

attachment_ids.description: Ids from `POST /attachments`, uploaded before the message that carries them. Up to 20.

parameters.description: Any string unique to this attempt, reused on its retries. A repeat with the same key and the same request returns the first answer with `Idempotent-Replay: true` and does nothing — no second email. The same key with a different request is a `409`. Kept for 24 hours; a failure is not kept, so a retry after one runs.

get.description: Counted from the event log rather than from the messages: a message row says what was sent, and whether it bounced is something the provider told us afterwards. `identity_id` narrows it to one mailbox, which is the question worth asking when you run several — reputation belongs to the address that sent the mail. `pod_id` narrows it to one pod, which is the question a platform asks: sending reputation is isolated per pod, so this is the scope that isolation is claimed at, and the response carries `reputation.sending` — `paused` is the provider having suspended that pod and nobody else. `delivery_rate` is null rather than zero when nothing was sent. An unknown parameter is refused rather than ignored.
